(Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) Ruhter grew up in the Wood River Valley, where she enjoyed her own high school French classes largely because of a passion for the French language and culture her teacher displayed. Ruhter then attended Boise State as a French major, where she felt welcomed and challenged by the faculty. “I felt really supported by the world language department,” Ruhter said. She looked forward to studying abroad in France for a full immersion experience, but the COVID-19 pandemic got in the way. In the meantime, Ruhter student taught at Capital, where the current French teacher was set to move on. She applied for the job before heading off to Brittany France, to spend two months working on a rural farm. It was difficult at first for Ruhter to speak the language she had only studied academically, but after some encouragement from the farmer she worked for, Ruhter dove into the language. “When I started talking, I felt like I couldn’t stop,” Ruhter said. The experience helped Ruhter understand the culture and language she spent eight years studying. “I was really inspired by how the small communities work together to support each other and keep going,” Ruhter said. Creating community has become central to Ruhter’s teaching style. Madame Ruhter’s French favorites: Book: Chanson Douce by Leïla Slimani (published as The Perfect Nanny in the U.S.) Movie: The Count of Monte Cristo (2024) Song: Princesse Chaos (Yoa) Ruhter returned to Boise and started her first year of teaching, which was “kind of awful.” “Your first year is probably not going to be your best year teaching,” Ruhter said. She taught a combined class at language proficiency levels 3-5 and in Advanced Placement French. She only survived with the help of her support system. Her learning coach helped with lesson plans, the school’s Spanish teacher was her emotional support, and her friend who teaches special education helped her differentiate lessons. “It’s just a really cool and collaborative community,” Ruhter said of Capital High. items.body: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Colonel Reginald Rodney Myers , who was born in Boise, earned the MOH for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lieutenant Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the MOH for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington , 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos. I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the Cemetery. That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project. Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an Act of Congress. It does not have Congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead. Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the Cemetery. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed building the Pentagon in that location. He changed his mind after being convinced that it would obliterate the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. The explanation for the arch must lie elsewhere. Trump admitted last October that the monument was intended to honor “me” but later claimed it was to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. As he has continued to take flak for the project, Trump and his lackeys now contend it is required for the national defense. We already have a national defense project in the grand ballroom adjacent to the White House, but that does not seem to be sufficient in the president’s mind. In a shameful attempt to get around building restrictions, he now claims the arch will be laden with drones, snipers and machine guns so as to protect Washington from attack. If he had the slightest understanding of military tactics, he would understand that his arch would make an indefensible sitting-duck target. Not everyone is keen for Trump’s vanity arch. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind. The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term. Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress , won governorships in most states and made headway in state legislatures . Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats gain six legislative seats — flipping competitive districts But by the time the national blue wave — or tsunami, as some are calling it — hit Idaho, the tide had turned it into a ripple. Idaho Democrats made modest gains. They swept full control of three legislative districts, gaining six more legislative seats , a shift that does little to chip away at Republicans’ supermajority control of the Legislature. And a closer look at election results shows that across the board, Democrats captured slightly more votes against Republican incumbents in statewide office and congress , who easily won reelection. But in all of those races, Democratic victory was still far off. No Democrat has won a statewide office in the state since 2002, and the last Democratic congressman in Idaho served in 2010. If Democrats want to upset decades of Idaho political history by winning a top of the ticket race, they have a long way to go. On average, Democrats gained 6 points of the vote share in federal and state races compared to the last time those offices were up for election. Still, Idaho Democrats this year were an average of 27 points behind Republicans, according to an analysis of election results by the Idaho Capital Sun. Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler wasn’t surprised that the blue wave didn’t carry Democrats through in Idaho. “Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said in an interview. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.” The Idaho Democratic Party also boasted another gain: Democrats got more of the vote in 67 legislative races than they did in 2024. This year’s election results are unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. items.body: Ada County election workers process hundreds of absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, more than a third of votes in Tuesday’s election were cast before Election Day. Over 290,000 of the more than 731,000 ballots cast in the election were through early and absentee voting, according to data from the Idaho secretary of state’s office. That’s 100,000 more of those types of voting than were submitted during the state’s last election for statewide offices in 2022, according to the state election agency. Those forms of voting — available without a need to state a reason — allow voters to cast ballots either in person or by mail before Election Day. (Technically, some of these absentee ballots were submitted on Election Day. In Idaho, absentee ballots may be submitted until polls close at 8 p.m. local time on Election Day.) Looking at state election data , the political makeup of the voters who cast ballots through early and absentee voting largely mirrors the state’s pool of more than 1 million registered voters , state data shows. With one caveat: Democrats vote early and absentee at higher rates. Here’s how it breaks down: About 59% of early and absentee voters this election were Republicans, which is slightly below the party affiliation of all registered voters, which is nearly 62% Republican. Unaffiliated voters make up nearly 22.3% of early and absentee voters, which is slightly lower than their nearly 24.6% share of Idaho’s total registered voters. Democrats make up nearly 18% of early and absentee voters. That’s a bigger rate of Idaho’s total registered Democrats, which is nearly 12%. Voters affiliated with third parties — the Constitution and Libertarian parties — make up a combined 0.76% of Idaho’s absentee voters. They make up less than 1.5% of all registered voters. There is also an age skew. Older voters, who make up most of Idaho’s total voters, vote early and absentee at higher rates than younger voters, the data show. Voters at least 45 years old make up 61.8% of the state’s registered voters, but cast 79% of the state’s early and absentee ballots this election. Voters age 44 and younger voted absentee and early less this year. They make up nearly 38.2% of registered voters, but just 21% of this year’s pre-Election Day votes. Voters aged 18 to 29 appeared the least likely to vote absentee and early this year. They cast only 7% of ballots early and absentee. But they make up 15.5% of registered voters, a higher share of the state’s overall voter pool than Idahoans age 75 and older, who make up nearly 13.8% of registered voters. It’s too early to tell how each of these demographics turned out to the polls this year. The secretary of state’s office hasn’t yet released more detailed information on the voters who showed up on Election Day. The U.S. Attorney's Office charged King with assault. (Screenshot from video) A Washington D.C. Superior Court judge has ordered the Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to an incident in May in which guards members detained a woman outside her home. D.C. resident Anna King filed a separate $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard in July for injuries and distress she said she experienced when she was detained on May 8. Members of the Gem State’s National Guard have been in the nation’s Capital since February as part of a Joint Task Force, although there was no public announcement of the deployment until after King filed her claim, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Under the direction of D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro at a hearing Thursday, the Idaho National Guard, D.C. National Guard and U.S. Department of Defense will have to produce, or explain why they can’t produce, documents related to the detainment of King. King wrote in her tort claim against the Idaho National Guard that the troops did not explain why they were detaining her or provide a warrant when they approached her that evening. A video of the incident shows three men in National Guard uniforms approaching King, who had been sitting on a bench outside her apartment. King told the guards members not to touch her. She walked toward the steps to go back into her apartment, but the troops blocked her, the video showed. Two of them pinned her against the ground and secured her wrists behind her back. The U.S. government charged King with two counts of misdemeanor assault on a police officer on May 9. In August, the U.S. Attorney’s Office added three more charges of simple assault. The charges stem from alleged assaults on May 6. King pleaded not guilty and asked for a trial. King’s attorney, Jeffrey Nestler, said the Idaho National Guard provided one document, but the legal team felt it wasn’t sufficient. King’s attorneys asked for all reports, records, communications, directives and other documents from the Idaho National Guard related to King. Di Toro agreed, and ordered the prosecutor to ensure the entities produce relevant documents. According to court documents and Nestler, the Idaho National Guard members who detained King on May 8 said they had “prior run-ins” with King and had been ordered to detain her. “We’re here now in the part of the law that requires the government to do more than just ask questions, so I’m going to direct you to actually spend a little more time trying to understand whether prior to May 6, the Idaho National Guard had what the defense is calling a run-in with Ms. King,” Di Toro told Assistant United States Attorney Vanessa Jacobsen Thursday. As of Nov. 6, there are 27 Idaho National Guard troops in Washington D.C. There are more than 3,000 National Guard members from other states and territories. King is a former Army captain and Purple Heart and Bronze Star recipient, according to a press release announcing her tort claim. “As a trained combat veteran, I never imagined that armed National Guard members would attack, injure, and traumatize me at my home,” King said in the press release. “We are not at war with Americans, and my porch is not a war zone.” The trial in the case against King is scheduled to start July 27, 2027. items.summary: The Idaho School Boards Association passed nine resolutions at its annual meeting on Friday, urging the 2027 Legislature to preserve local control and fulfill its constitutional responsibility to provide adequate funding for all public schools. items.body: The Idaho School Boards Association passed nine resolutions at its annual meeting on Friday, urging the 2027 Legislature to preserve local control and fulfill its constitutional responsibility to provide adequate funding for all public schools. School board members from across the state gathered in Boise to elect leadership, approve bylaws and pass resolutions that will guide the association’s lobbying efforts throughout the coming legislative session. “The ISBA legislative platform gives our association a unified voice as we advocate for Idaho public schools,” said outgoing President Jason Sevy, a Marsing trustee. With a bang of his gavel at the end of Friday’s general session, Sevy ended his time as president and handed the reins over to Eric Smallwood, chair of the Twin Falls school board, who has served as president-elect for the past year. Members elected Brett Plummer of Challis as the new president-elect and Pam Wagoner of Middleton as vice president. They were the only candidates for each position. Click to view slideshow. “My priorities are clear: Strengthening board collaboration across the districts,” Plummer said in a prepared speech before the vote. “We’re stronger when we share ideas, resources and solutions.” But the main event on Friday was voting on eight pre-submitted resolutions and one introduced on the floor that addressed the Idaho School Benefit Trust shortfall . They all passed. Votes are weighted based on the size of the district and are not a direct one-to-one correlation with the number of trustees. Here’s the ISBA’s new legislative platform. Resolution No. 1: Human growth and development video Submitted by the Boise School District Passed: 8,866-112 (98.7%) Boise trustee Paul Bennion presented a resolution that asks the Legislature to clean up “conflicting and impractical” language around human growth and development instruction, in particular a requirement to show a fetal development video in classrooms. Public schools have had one year to implement a law — enacted through Senate Bill 1046 in 2025 — requiring that students in grades 5-12 watch a high-definition ultrasound video during instruction on human growth and development. The bill has created “confusion for parents and schools, repeated notices, repeated video presentations in courses where the content is not instructionally relevant, and timelines that do not fit school scheduling,” the resolution states. “The resolution seeks clarity, local flexibility, practical timelines, and consistent parent rights so districts and charter schools can comply with state law without unnecessary disruption to instruction.” Resolution No. 2: Statewide educational resource development program Submitted by the Council School District Passed: 7,881-927 (89.5%) Jen Hamaker, a trustee for Council School District, said it’s time to think outside the box when it comes to funding and enriching our children’s education. While a handful of Idaho’s largest school districts might have staff dedicated to finding funding opportunities, like grants and donations, most small and rural districts don’t. This resolution proposes a “statewide educational resource development program” that could help school districts compete for funding. “No Idaho student’s educational opportunities should be limited simply because their school district lacks the staff, expertise or capacity to pursue resources that already exist,” says the resolution’s statement of purpose. items.body: Dozens of school trustees were granted an impromptu session with Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron on Wednesday to discuss the collapse of an employee health insurance program. Nothing has changed — they all had to pay their share of the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall — but they had the opportunity to get some questions answered during their annual Idaho School Boards Association conference in Boise. Cameron provided some new details about what happened to the trust, as his department is conducting an investigation that is expected to wrap up this month. Those managing the trust set rates too low and were counting on a “hope, a wing and a prayer” to get through the latest benefit year. Instead, their plan didn’t work. The trust became insolvent and a district court judge has taken all authority away from the trust’s leaders and granted full power to Cameron to rehabilitate the benefit trust. “The nightmare took place really over a couple-year period of time,” Cameron said. “The trust had assumed the risk, and the risk occurred.” Sen.-elect Soñia Galaviz, D-Boise, asked Cameron to speak at the ISBA conference and said he had to rearrange his schedule to attend. The hourlong presentation and Q&A on Wednesday was tacked on to the end of the day’s scheduled events. Attendees were informed about it at lunchtime. As Galaviz introduced Cameron, she said he understands what is at stake and he knows that “our hearts are heavy right now.” “Dean Cameron is a friend,” she said. items.title: College-course enrollment at Idaho’s online learning program falls by nearly half
items.summary: Enrollment in college-level courses provided by the Idaho Digital Learning Alliance fell 46% in summer and fall 2026 compared with the same period last year, as new fees took effect after a major cut to the state-funded online learning program. In the summer and fall of 2025, IDLA recorded 5,540 dual credit enrollments. In 2026, it recorded 2,980 dual credit enrollments in the same time period. ID
items.body: Enrollment in college-level courses provided by the Idaho Digital Learning Alliance fell 46% in summer and fall 2026 compared with the same period last year, as new fees took effect after a major cut to the state-funded online learning program. In the summer and fall of 2025, IDLA recorded 5,540 dual credit enrollments. In 2026, it recorded 2,980 dual credit enrollments in the same time period. IDLA Superintendent Jeff Simmons discussed the decline during a Thursday workshop at the Idaho School Boards Association’s annual convention in Boise. A decline in funding has forced IDLA to draw on its savings to serve more students than the program is funded to accommodate. “That’s certainly not something we can do every year,” Simmons said of using savings to serve more students than its funding allows. IDLA is a state-funded online learning program that offers virtual courses to Idaho students, including classes that let high schoolers earn college credits. The decline in those courses could limit student access to affordable college classes, particularly in rural communities where schools rely on IDLA to expand course offerings. Simmons said the declines are largely because of course fees schools and students must pay after legislators slashed about half of the virtual program’s budget and limited its scope during the 2026 legislative session. “We used to waive the course fee for a dual credit class, so we didn’t charge a fee,” Simmons told several trustees and school administrators Thursday. Previously, students could use Advanced Opportunities dollars to cover the cost of college credits when taking dual credit courses through IDLA. A new law requires IDLA to charge a fee of $40 for classes that are a graduation requirement or $100 for classes that aren’t. In a survey of rural schools, Simmons said 70% of responding districts cited the course fee as the reason students weren’t taking dual credit courses. “I don’t think this was an intentional outcome of the legislation,” Simmons said. Simmons doesn’t know where students are turning to take college courses instead. To find out, “we’re trying to do some collaborative data collection, so we can bring a full picture back to the State Board and the state Legislature,” he said. Brett Arnzen, board chair at the Highland School District in Craigmont, said his district will have to make changes if IDLA “continues on the path it does.” The district works IDLA’s fees into its longtime supplemental levy. But as the levy becomes more difficult to pass — gaining approval by just three votes last year and 150 votes this year — Arnzen worries about asking for more. The enrollment picture extends beyond college courses. Over the summer, IDLA enrolled 8,608 students – 2,200 above what it’s funded to serve. Currently, 12,056 students are enrolled for the fall semester – 806 over what the statewide online school is funded for. This year, IDLA received state funds to serve 32,000 students. The program enrolled 56,000 students last year, before the Legislature cut $13.4 million from IDLA’s $26 million budget. IDLA’s leaders are working with state superintendent Debbie Critchfield and Gov. Brad Little to “right-size” the budget for next fiscal year, Simmons said. items.body: More than 60 school trustees and administrators crowded a large meeting room at the Boise Centre Thursday morning as Kimberly Superintendent Luke Schroeder and sixth-grade teacher Brad Carlson detailed their district’s armed staff policy. “If we can delay that shooter by five seconds, we may have just saved some of these lives,” said Schroeder. Schroeder started the presentation with some statistics: On average, someone gets shot every 4.7 seconds in a mass shooting. Eighty percent of the killing is going to happen in the first 30 seconds. Before teaching sixth grade, Carlson was a U.S. Army Cavalry Scout and southern California police officer who trained officers and teachers to handle active shootings. He laid out the tactics and procedures Kimberly uses. “My goal for this is not to create gunfighters and gunslingers. The goal is to mitigate a threat before it ever shows up to our school,” Carlson said. Training against school shooters has also become more difficult in recent years, he said. “Bad guys are learning our tactics, techniques and procedures,” Carlson said. “They know the doors are locked; they’re now ballistically breaching. They’re shooting out windows – it just happened in Bend, Oregon.” Kimberly School District Superintendent Luke Schroeder, left, and sixth grade teacher Brad Carlson, right, speak to trustees and administrators in a workshop on arming school staff at the Idaho School Boards Association Annual Convention on Nov. 5, 2026 in Boise. items.body: A “Stop Prop 1” sign leans up against the wall during a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Boise, Idaho. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with 2026 general election outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The failure of Idaho’s proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 in Tuesday’s general election was met with celebration and concern as the state’s abortion ban remains fully in place. Idaho voters rejected the ballot measure with 55.94% of the vote, according to the unofficial statewide results. Election officials will certify results by Nov. 24. Dorothy Moon, chairwoman of the Idaho Republican Party, addresses partygoers at the Idaho Republican Party’s general election watch party on Nov. 5, 2024, in Meridian. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “We defeated Prop 1, and that was the biggest issue facing our state,” Idaho GOP Chairwoman Dorothy Moon told the Idaho Capital Sun in a phone interview. Idaho’s result contrasted with Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada and Virginia, where voters approved ballot initiatives to protect abortion or rejected a measure to reinstate an abortion ban, Stateline reported. The Idaho initiative’s supporters expressed concern about healthcare access in the state as many physicians say the abortion ban limits their ability to perform their job. “I think that Idaho failed its communities in (not) pushing to change restrictions that affect all of us,” said Dr. Jessica Evans-Wall, a Treasure Valley emergency medicine physician. “What I see in the emergency department is that these bans on providing healthcare don’t just affect patients who are pregnant and their families, they affect our whole community.” The proposed measure would have repealed Idaho’s strict abortion laws, legalizing the procedure up to fetal viability or in cases of emergency and enumerated rights related to access to reproductive healthcare. Under Idaho’s laws, physicians face felony prison sentences and licensing penalties if they perform nearly any abortion, with exemptions to protect the life of the mother in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho GOP, religious groups strongly opposed proposition The Idaho Republican Central Committee vocally opposed Prop 1, and county party central committees spent campaign funds to oppose it. Opponents formed Stop Prop 1 in response to the initiative proposal. Moon, the Idaho GOP chair, said the initiative was likely a motivating factor for many Idahoans to show up to the polls Tuesday. “All the churches jumped on board. Every demographic jumped on board to make sure that we do not allow abortion on demand in this state, so I think that that was the driving issue,” Moon said. A number of elected Republicans also spoke against the ballot measure. “We are so grateful to Idahoans for resoundingly defeating Prop 1,” Idaho state House leaders said in a written joint statement. “Idaho voters held the line against the extreme abortion agenda, against the lies and deceptions of the Prop 1 campaign, and proved once again why Idaho values are second to none. items.body: Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcom Kenyatta, a Democrat, speaks Wednesday at a party celebrating Democratic control of state government in Harrisburg. Across the country, Democrats flipped hundreds of state legislative seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) The blue wave that swept across Tuesday’s midterm election will deliver Democrats new power over state government, giving them the opportunity to advance long-sought policy changes. Democrats flipped hundreds of seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Democratic lawmakers from multiple states pledged to use their new statehouse power to attack rising prices, protect reproductive rights, pass new gun safety measures and grow the housing supply. The changed landscape also gives state Democratic leaders more power to oppose the agenda of President Donald Trump, said Marc Farinella, senior advisor to the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy. That may mean opposing Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts, Farinella said, or bolstering state funding of Medicaid and food stamps, both of which have faced significant federal cuts under Trump. Legislating will prove much easier in states with newly won Democratic trifectas, where the party controls both chambers and the governor’s office. Those states include Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. But newly divided governments in other states — Iowa, Ohio, Georgia, Texas — could result in gridlock. Following the midterms, state legislatures will see their biggest leadership shakeup in years, as the National Conference of State Legislatures expects nearly half of state chambers to have new leaders next session. “None of us have ever been in a majority, so it’s a big learning curve,” said Arizona state Rep. Nancy Gutierrez, assistant House minority leader. She said Democrats, who will control Phoenix for the first time in 60 years, are connecting with their counterparts from other states, such as Colorado, that have swung from red to blue. The Pennsylvania state Senate flipped to Democratic control for the first time since 1978, handing the party a resounding trifecta after Gov. Josh Shapiro sailed to reelection. Already, Shapiro and Democratic state lawmakers have pledged to revive a slew of policies that had previously passed the state House but died in the Republican-controlled Senate. Those include raising the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour, codifying abortion rights, passing a law to allow survivors of sexual abuse to sue their abusers and increasing funding for mass transit. “I think here in Pennsylvania we made very, very clear at the state level and the federal level that we are rejecting Donald Trump’s policies and we want to see costs come down,” Shapiro said Wednesday. “And now you’ve got an opportunity to see that happen in Harrisburg and in Washington.” At the same time, Farinella said, this week’s “historically forceful rebuke of Trump and his agenda” will prompt an as yet undetermined response from Republicans. After a decade of near-total control by Trump and the MAGA movement, the decisive GOP losses could free some Republicans to return to more centrist policies, he said. “To me, it’s the big outstanding question coming out of the election,” Farinella said. “How will the congressional Republicans and how will the Republicans in state legislatures now feel about the latitude they have or don’t have in terms of their own policy preferences?” Progress or gridlock? items.title: Democrats listened to voters’ affordability concerns, party chair says
items.summary: The chair of the Idaho Democratic Party credits Tuesday’s sweep of three swing districts in the Legislature to listening to voters over the past year and focusing on solutions to challenges they are facing. Democrats picked up one seat in the Senate and five in the House. The party will now hold 21 seats in the Idaho Legislature in January, but Republicans still carry a supermajority with 84 seats
items.body: The chair of the Idaho Democratic Party credits Tuesday’s sweep of three swing districts in the Legislature to listening to voters over the past year and focusing on solutions to challenges they are facing. Democrats picked up one seat in the Senate and five in the House. The party will now hold 21 seats in the Idaho Legislature in January, but Republicans still carry a supermajority with 84 seats. C hair Lauren Necochea said the six flipped seats will put Democrats in a better position to make good policy and stop bad bills that harm Idahoans. “What we heard from people is that affordability, healthcare — those regular kitchen table economic concerns — are what are on the top of people’s minds,” Necochea told EdNews in a Wednesday afternoon phone call. She said Democrats have solutions in that regard, while Republicans just shrug and hope the free market will take care of it. Over the next two months before the 2027 session begins, she said the Democratic caucus will work to formalize an agenda based on what the candidates ran on. Democrats want to remove the state’s grocery tax, bring back the child tax credit, which expired in January , and restore cuts to Medicaid. Necochea said the party also wants to end “sweetheart deals” with data centers and to stop giving tax breaks to wealthy individuals and profitable corporations. Lauren Necochea, chair of the Idaho Democratic Party, during an interview on Monday, Dec. 15, 2025, at the party’s headquarters in Boise. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) The six new seats could also help Democrats block increases to Idaho’s $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit for students enrolled in non-public schools. House Bill 93, which created the tax credit in 2025, passed 42-28 in the House and 20-15 in the Senate. “We’re spending $50 million a year on vouchers while we’re cutting Medicaid so deeply that moms are getting letters that their child with a disability is going to have their therapies limited,” Necochea said. Democrats currently hold three of 20 seats on the powerful Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. Necochea said Tuesday’s gains mean Democrats should get one more. “If there is justice in the world, we should have another seat,” she said. “We’ll be holding 20% of the House, and we should have seats on JFAC accordingly.” Nationally, Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, but all federal seats in Idaho remain in Republican control. Necochea said the national landscape motivated swing district voters because they saw just how far Republicans would go to rubber-stamp the Trump administration, which she said has devastated farmers and made everything more expensive. “We don’t have a single Republican leader in Idaho who has spoken out against any of these really harmful actions,” she said. When asked if there is a particular seat Necochea is most proud that Democrats won on Tuesday, she said she is “proud of all of our candidates.”

items.body: An election worker speaks to a voter in South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho’s general election on Tuesday, some voters were voting hours after polls had closed in the state’s second most populated county. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, attends a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Voting bled into Wednesday. The last voter in Canyon County cast their ballot at 12:20 a.m., Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said in an interview Wednesday morning. In Idaho, polls close at 8 p.m. local time. But voters can still cast votes if they are in line by the deadline. And in Canyon County in southwest Idaho, some voters waited in lines for more than four hours, McGrane said. The lines there, driven by high turnout and long ballots, were one of his biggest challenges of the night. “The interesting thing, both visiting with the poll workers and watching some of the news outlets that visited out there, the voters were really patient, really kind, very determined to want to be able to cast their vote. I think it was incredible just to see the sense of community out there,” McGrane said. “Regardless, I think we owe it to the voters, and we’ve certainly heard some feedback just in terms of how frustrating that was. We want to make sure the voting process goes smoothly.” The lines were a sign of a bigger trend. In Tuesday’s general election for statewide offices, congressional seats, legislative seats and ballot measures, including an abortion ballot initiative, Idaho voters turned out at high rates. A midterm record high of 731,980 voters cast ballots, based on initial voter turnout data from the Secretary of State’s Office. Overall, it seems likely that registered voters turned out in the high 60% range to vote in the election, McGrane said. Besides the long lines in Canyon County, the day was fairly smooth, he said. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Abortion ballot initiative drove voter turnout, experts say Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban, seemed to drive many voters to the polls. Nearly 99% of voters cast ballots in that race — more than any statewide ballot measure. Voters rejected it, with nearly 56% voting no, according to unofficial election results . “I do think the fact that more ballots were cast on Prop 1 than any of the other statewide races indicate that it was driving some people to the polls, particularly to vote on that issue,” Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler said in an interview. The drive to turn out was likely twofold, she said: Voters tend to care deeply about abortion and reproductive healthcare issues, and there was active campaigning from both sides. But the blue wave in midterms across the country — where Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, and won control of some state legislatures and most governorships — didn’t extend to Idaho. Republican incumbents in all statewide offices and the state’s congressional delegation all easily secured reelection. Kettler wasn’t surprised. “Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.” Still, Democrats saw some success in Idaho as they picked up six seats in the state Legislature, which remains under Republican supermajority control. In those wins, Democrats secured full control of three swing districts. Tuesday’s election results in Idaho won’t become official until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers on Nov. 24. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Nationwide results for abortion ballot initi
items.body: A “Stop Prop 1” sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Boise, Idaho. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated. Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the approval of Proposition 1 and 44% voting in favor, nearly the inverse of Missouri’s outcome, where 55% of voters struck down an amendment that would have reinstated the ban that was overturned through a ballot initiative in 2024. O ther abortion-related measures were on the ballot in Nevada and Virginia, two states where abortion is already accessible until 24 weeks and 26 weeks of pregnancy, respectively. Voters in both of those states passed constitutional amendments ensuring the right to abortion. The outcome in Idaho ensures the state’s abortion ban remains intact. The ban prohibits abortion at any stage of pregnancy with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. Blaine Conzatti, president of the Idaho Family Policy Center, the organization that helped craft the ban and campaigned against the initiative, said in a statement that “abortion advocates fundamentally misunderstood Idaho.” “As we proved last night, a broad majority of Idaho voters support our pro-life laws,” Conzatti said. “This is what happens when Christians speak out and get engaged — we win.” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families and lead organizer of the initiative, said in a statement that more than $1.3 million in donations from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and the Catholic Diocese of Boise fueled a disinformation campaign about what the law would do. “We’re encouraging Idahoans to reach out to their lawmakers, particularly those politicians who encouraged voters to reject Prop 1 and wait for a legislative fix, and demand needed exceptions in the coming session,” Folwell said. A federal appeals court ruled on Oct. 30 that Idaho’s law does not include exceptions for a pregnant person whose physical or mental health is in jeopardy by continuing the pregnancy, a situation that Idaho doctors have repeatedly said puts them in a position to feel compelled to wait until a patient’s life is in danger before acting. A peer-reviewed study published in 2025 in JAMA showed 114 OB-GYNs left Idaho or stopped practicing obstetrics between August 2022 and December 2024, the first two years after the ban took effect. That number represents 43% of the 268 physicians practicing obstetrics statewide. Several of those who left have said publicly that the ban made it more difficult to do their jobs without fear of criminal prosecution. Providers found guilty of violating the ban face up to five years in prison, the revocation of their medical license and up to $20,000 in civil penalties. Many doctors who have continued to practice obstetrics and gynecology in Idaho say the loss of those providers has increased their workload to a stressful and at times dangerous degree. In the months leading up to the vote, Idaho women shared their stories of needing to seek care in other states, including Utah , because of fatal fetal anomalies, along with others who said their care during a miscarriage was delayed, causing dangerous infections. With the failure of the ballot measure, pregnant patients who need an abortion will continue to need to seek care in other states. items.body: The Idaho Legislature unanimously approved placing the non-binding poll of state guns on the ballot through House Bill 932 this year. (Yves Adams/Getty Images) In a non-binding vote, Idaho voters nominated a lever-action rifle, dubbed the “Gun that Won the West” to be the state’s official gun. The gun, the Winchester Model 1873, had the backing from about 31% of Idaho voters, the highest share of any of the guns on the ballot in Tuesday’s general election, according to unofficial results from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office at 12:30 p.m. Wednesday. All of Idaho’s 44 counties were reporting election results by then. A digital representation of a Winchester 1873. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office) The vote tees up a decision by the Idaho Legislature to potentially join 10 other states that have official state guns. Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. None of the six guns — placed on the ballot in a unanimous vote by the Legislature — received a majority vote. Here’s how all the guns on the list fared with voters this year: Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40): 31.1% of the vote, or 164,394 votes. Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30): 25.32% of the vote, or 133,859 votes. 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver, or “Peacemaker,” (.45 Colt): 15.26% of the vote, or 80,699 votes. Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06): 12.45% of the vote, or 65,818 votes. Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP): 8.78% of the vote, or 46,405 votes. M1 Garand rifle (.30-06): 7.09% of the vote, or 37,500 votes. None of the guns on Idaho’s ballot have developmental ties to the state, unlike the official guns in some other states, like Utah . If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said in an interview last month that he pushed to put the question on the ballot to help drum up voter turnout. The measure, called an advisory question, had the lowest share of ballots cast of any of the statewide ballot measures. About 70% of voters cast votes in the race for the state gun, out of the more than 731,000 of voters who turned out to the polls for this election, unofficial election results show. Nearly 99% of voters cast votes on Proposition 1, a ballot initiative — which voters rejected — that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban. About 97% of Idaho voters cast ballots on each of the constitutional amendments: A successful one to declare English as the state’s official language , and a failed one that would’ve revoked voters’ powers to legalize marijuana and other drugs . Idaho voters turned out to vote at high rates this year in a midterm election, when voters tend to vote less. About 69% of the state’s registered voters cast ballots, early data show. But election officials expect the turnout rate to drop several points as they factor in voters who registered to vote on Election Day. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

Brad Little, left, speaks to Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke at the governor’s Nov. 3, 2026, election night watch party in Boise. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) Now, let’s not lose sight of the big picture. Tuesday was still a very good night for Idaho Republicans. The GOP again swept every statewide race — with no after-midnight vote count suspense. Idaho will again send an all-Republican delegation to Congress, as Sen. Jim Risch and Reps. Mike Simpson and Russ Fulcher dodged a wave election that flipped the House and Senate to the Democrats. Last and certainly not least, the Republicans’ all-in opposition to Proposition 1 appeared to pay dividends. Party leadership and key Republican officeholders banded together against Prop 1, and 56% of voters rejected a voter initiative seeking to overturn Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. So, a predictably red election night in Idaho? Generally yes, but not exactly typical. This will come as no comfort to Democratic loyalists who are comparing Idaho’s results with the stunning upsets in GOP fortresses such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas (and perhaps, depending on the final tallies, Mississippi and Alaska). Nor will this comfort Proposition 1 supporters, after what became an unsurprisingly bitter campaign over reproductive rights and restrictions. Idaho progressives were mourning on Wednesday, while many Idaho conservatives were celebrating. But despite everything that went well for the Idaho GOP Tuesday — and there was a lot of that — this wasn’t another regular Republican rout. For starters, the Democrats picked up six legislative seats , one in the Senate, five in the House. On the surface, this only changes the Legislature around the margins. Republicans still hold 28 of the Senate’s 35 seats, and 56 of the 70 spots in the House. But let’s look under the surface. Six additional legislative seats should give the Democrats some additional spots on key Statehouse committees. The first place to watch: the budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. Four years ago, House Speaker Mike Moyle assigned nine Republicans and one Democrat to JFAC, arguing that Democrats had long been overrepresented on the Legislature’s most powerful committee. By sheer math, the Democrats now have one-fifth of the House’s seats, which could again get them a second spot on the House’s side of JFAC. In a similar vein, Democrats might wind up with additional seats on the Senate State Affairs Committee and, possibly, the House Education Committee. Idaho State Sen. items.body: A "Stop Prop 1" sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, held at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday. The voter-led ballot initiative received 43.68% of the vote, or 286,909 votes in the 2026 general election, as of 2:37 a.m. on Wednesday. More than 56.32% voted against it, early results showed. The proposition needed a simple majority of votes to pass. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group formed to author and support the initiative, conceded that it did not pass in a press release sent just after 12:20 a.m. Idahoans United for Women and Families Executive Director Melanie Folwell speaks about Proposition 1 at the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings rally at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Jim Max for the Idaho Capital Sun) “This is a tremendous, frankly gutting, loss, especially for the women, families, and physicians of Idaho,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a press release. “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election. And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.” Election officials were still counting ballots early into Wednesday morning. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. The initiative would’ve repealed Idaho’s strict abortion ban, which outlaws nearly all abortions, except to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester when a police report is provided. Idaho’s ban carries felony prison sentences and licensing penalties for doctors who perform abortions outside of the exemptions, as well as possible civil lawsuits for a minimum of $20,000. Opponents of the ballot initiative argue that it is the state’s prerogative to protect fetuses’ lives, and that Idaho’s exemptions are sufficient to protect the mother’s life. The Idaho GOP, the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative. Opponents formed a group called Stop Prop 1 in response to the proposed initiative. “The people of Idaho have spoken,” Stop Prop 1 communications director Mary Strow said in a press release. “They saw through the smokescreen of deception and barrage of out-of-state funded ads that sought to rewrite our laws and reshape our values. Idaho is and will always be a state that values life and protects the unborn.” Idahoans United for Women and Families formed in 2024 to explore ways to restore abortion access in the state in response to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, which triggered Idaho’s bans. Idahoans United in July turned in nearly 110,000 signatures to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to qualify for the 2026 general election ballot. In Idaho, to qualify for the general election, supporters must collect signatures from at least 6% of the registered voters statewide and from at least 6% of the registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. To achieve the 6% statewide total, supporters needed 70,725 verified signatures. Share your ‘Cece story’: Boise State’s Andrus Center will host ‘History Harvest’ for book project The Andrus for Idaho: History Harvest event, hosted by the Boise State University Andrus Center, includes several panel discussions and presentations from some of the people who knew Andrus best, as well as an “Antiques Roadshow”-style History Harvest, which encourages Idahoans to bring in photos, memorabilia, artifacts, letters and oral histories from Andrus’ time in office to have them documented and archived. The two-day event will begin at 9 a.m. Friday and 9:45 a.m. Saturday at SPACE in Boise State University’s Albertsons Library, 1865 Friendship Lane on BSU’s campus. Both days of the event will go through the afternoon, and the public can join the activities at anytime throughout the day. The Andrus Center is also looking for volunteers to help with the event, including set-up beforehand, guiding visitors and helping at informational stations during the event and tear down and archival work afterward. To register as a volunteer, fill out this Google form online . Who was Cecil Andrus? Cecil Andrus, the last Democrat to serve as Idaho’s governor, died at age 85 in 2017. He was the only person to serve four terms – a nonconsecutive 14 years – as Idaho governor. But his service to the state and nation extended far beyond that one role. After serving in the U.S. Navy during the Korean War, he was concerned about the direction of Idaho’s public schools and ran for the state Senate in 1960 at just 28 years old, winning the seat. That began a longtime tenure in state politics, with his first stint as Idaho governor from 1971-1977. Serving as governor would eventually help prepare him for his role as U.S. secretary of the Interior in the Jimmy Carter administration from 1977-1981. He again was elected Idaho governor from 1987-1995. As Idaho’s population changes and grows, Emily Wakild, the Cecil D. Andrus endowed chairwoman for environment and public lands in the School of the Environment, College of Arts and Sciences, said the event is a way to bring the state’s history to life — and to capture the memories and items related to Andrus’ political life before it’s too late. Volunteers will be on-hand to scan photos, letters and other documents, while others will be available to record oral histories and personal stories about Andrus. items.body: Walking from one end of Meridian Technical Charter High to the other takes only about two minutes, as the entire building is only 19,000 square feet. However, within the 14 classrooms, students are learning curricula that could be taught at university level. Last week, Idaho Legislators joined representatives from the Idaho Charter School Association to tour Meridian Technical Charter High School (MTCHS) and Meridian Medical Arts Charter High School (MMACHS). After the tours, they sat for panels with students and parents. The schools are two different buildings that share the same campus. They both set students up for success after high school, but their specialties couldn’t be more different. At Meridian Technical Charter High School, students take introductory coding and networking lessons their freshman year. MTCHS is focused on providing a progressive, technical education experience. Apart from a regular academic course load, the school provides students with over 1,000 hours of technical training and specific training in personal and workplace skills. There are six different pathways with various focus areas provided at the school, including Computer, Networking, Media, Web, Software, and Electronics. MTCHS accepts only freshmen by a lottery due to the rigorous 4-year curriculum plan that starts with a rotation of the different pathways. At the end of their first year, they must choose one pathway to continue with until graduation. “If they don’t come in as a freshman, they’re so far behind because they start taking certifications their sophomore year,” said Craig Miller, Principal of MTCHS. items.body: Idaho Conservation League Executive Director Courtney Washburn Experienced conservationist and policy leader Courtney Washburn has been named the new executive director of the Idaho Conservation League, the league and its board of directors announced last month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Washburn succeeds previous Executive Director Justin Hayes, who announced last year he was taking a new position at the group American Rivers. The Idaho Conservation League is a more than 50-year-old nonprofit organization with a mission to protect clean air, clean water, land and wildlife. The new role represents a homecoming for Washburn, who previously served as the Idaho Conservation League’s community conservation director and statehouse lobbyist from 2006 to 2015. In her new role, Washburn is focusing on connecting and partnering with people and groups to take on the challenges of protecting Idaho. “I’m really focused on both growing the conservation community and connecting – or reconnecting, depending on how long people have lived in Idaho – with the conservation values and the actions that’s needed to protect this great state,” Washburn said in an interview Wednesday. “Progress would be to finally dispel the myth that people who care about conservation are associated with one party or another,” Washburn said. “I’d really like to see a durable kind of big tent. Everyone has a voice to speak up for their values, whether it be clean air, clean water, public lands.” “People care deeply about their state, and if you get to the core values, there are far less arguments, in my experience,” she added. Washburn also previously served as executive director for Conservation Voters for Idaho from 2015 to 2020. More recently, Washburn served as chief of staff for the city of Boise from 2020 to 2026, where she directed municipal operations, longterm planning and climate initiatives. Boise Dev reported in May that Boise Mayor Lauren McLean authorized a large severance payment for Washburn after Washburn left the city position. items.body: The Snake River runs through Idaho Falls. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho has periodically faced serious threats to its water sovereignty from an overreaching federal government. In the early 1950s, when Len Jordan was Idaho governor, the feds wanted to build a massive dam on the Snake River in Hells Canyon. That would have usurped Idaho control of its upstream waters. Jordan stopped the proposal, opting instead for the three existing Idaho Power company dams in order to protect Idaho’s control of those waters. The next water fight occurred after I was elected as Idaho attorney general in 1982. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights Idaho Power had just received an erroneous decision from the Idaho Supreme Court, giving the company practical control of Snake River waters above its Swan Falls Dam in Ada County. Gov. John Evans and I were able to work together behind the scenes and across the political aisle to defeat that threat. When we were able to get the conflict settled to the state’s advantage, the next federal threat raised its ugly head. In December 1987, Congress was on the verge of approving legislation that would have given the feds the ability to control the flow of Snake River waters above Deer Flats Wildlife Refuge in Canyon County. The matter was being handled behind closed doors in congressional offices. When my staff members learned that a political deal was being made to compromise the state’s interests, I blew the whistle, the Idaho water community erupted in anger, and the threat was brought to a screeching halt. Anyone interested in the details can check out pages 337-345 of my book on the subject – “ A Little Dam Problem .” The latest threat to Idaho’s water sovereignty surfaced less than two months ago. Shortly after it was announced that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected as a finalist for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus , the Trump administration launched an extremely troubling lawsuit challenging Idaho’s ability to “administer” the federal water right at the INL. In practical terms it means that, if there is a water shortage involving water rights in the INL vicinity, any reduction or mitigation would fall wholly upon the shoulders of other Idaho water users — farmers, fish producers and other folks dependent on those waters. The INL would be exempt. Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans The lawsuit was filed against Idaho in the federal court in Boise on Sept. 11, without any attendant publicity from either side. While the allegations focus primarily upon the INL water right, the complaint seeks much broader relief. The Trump administration wants “a declaration that the Idaho Department of Water Resources lacks the authority to administer federal water rights” and “an order permanently enjoining the Director of IDWR from exercising his authority” under any state law as to the United States or its agencies. In short, the administration is asking the court to prevent Idaho from administering federal water rights anywhere within state borders. This is wholly without precedent and contrary to the determination of rights in the Snake River Basin Adjudication . The agreement settling the Swan Falls water right fight called for filing a case in state court to adjudicate all water rights to Snake River Basin waters. That is, to quantify and prioritize those rights in court proceedings. Idaho specifically sought and received approval to include all federal water rights under a federal law, called the McCarran Amendment, that permits federal claims to be determined in a state court adjudication. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote
items.body: Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026. A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election. In an opinion released late Friday night , Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations. A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning . They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads. IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign. All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups. “Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote. Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge. VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party. An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs. “The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote. That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply. “However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.” Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads. “I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said. A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night. Memorandum Decision and Order Denying Motion For Prelimiary Injunction

items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Update: This story was updated at 5:10 p.m. on Oct. 30 with a comment from the plaintiff, Dr. Stacy Seyb. A federal appeals court panel ruled on Friday that Idaho’s abortion ban may continue to be fully enforced, including against a Boise doctor who challenged the ban’s lack of health exemption. A U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit panel ruled 2-1 to continue to block a lower court’s decision that would have prevented prosecution of maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb if he performed abortions in which he determined there were serious risks to the mother’s health or mental health. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. Seyb’s challenge, which argued Idaho’s abortion ban’s lack of exemptions to prevent serious harm to the mother’s health or death from self-harm were unconstitutional, will continue to be litigated in court. Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan said in the majority opinion that Seyb’s argument for a constitutional right to abortion as a health-saving measure or in cases of risk of self-harm were unlikely to align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade. “We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the majority decision said. “… Idaho has a strong interest in limiting abortions to those allowed under its law. This interest clearly outweighs the potential harm to Dr. Seyb of having to abide by Idaho’s law pending the resolution of this appeal.” Wardlaw concurred with the majority decision. Judge Marsha S. Berzon disagreed, writing that the high court’s decision only applied to elective abortions, and not when the procedure may be medically necessary or indicated. Berzon agreed with district court Judge B. Lynn Winmill, whose previous order argued there was likely a “fundamental right” to abortions to preserve the mother’s health. Berzon also argued that the risk of harm for Seyb’s patients was greater than that of the state’s. “… with the stay imposed by the majority in place, some women with serious pregnancy complications will during the pendency of this appeal be required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health,” Berzon wrote. “The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury.” Seyb said in a written statement, “Laws that criminalize abortion make pregnancy less safe.” “I will continue to advocate for the right of every patient to make important medical decisions without government interference,” he said. The conservative Christian advocacy group the Idaho Family Policy Center, which helped author Idaho’s abortion ban allowing civil lawsuits against doctors, celebrated Friday’s decision in a press release. “Pregnant mothers don’t have a constitutional right to abortion merely because they threaten to harm themselves,” Idaho Family Policy Center Blaine Conzatti said in the release. “Women in mental health crises need treatment, not abortion. This decision ensures that our pro-life laws here in Idaho will continue protecting both mother and baby.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: In a rare but legally required move, the Canyon County Board of County Commissioners on Thursday appointed naturopathic medical doctor Brett Butterfield to fill a vacancy on the Vallivue school board. If a school board in Idaho fails to fill a vacancy within 120 days, the local county commissioners are required to make the appointment. Trustee Toni Brinegar resigned on June 9, which was 142 days ago as of Thursday. “This is a statutory requirement,” Canyon County Chief Civil Deputy Aaron Bazzoli told the commissioners at Thursday’s meeting. He said the school district provided Butterfield’s name, but there were “some issues with how they went about the process.” Commissioner Leslie Van Beek thanked Bazzoli for putting on the record the county’s statutory authority to make the appointment. “I don’t know that the board has been asked — not in my tenure — to be the one that appoints a person for a vacancy on a school board,” she said. She then made a motion to appoint Butterfield. “We’re not here to overstep the wishes of the Vallivue school board,” Van Beek said. “For whatever reason, they had problems, so this was the name that surfaced as the candidate they wanted to fill that seat and I am in favor.” With the appointment secured, the five-member Vallivue school board is now back to full strength after two resignations this summer. items.body: The Snake River flows alongside the Idaho Falls greenbelt. (Photo courtesy of Hyo Lee/U.S. Department of Energy) Throughout history there has been one thing all Idahoans agreed on — water is the lifeblood of Idaho. Water has made our southern Idaho sagebrush country bloom with farms and ranches, and water has been crucial for the protection of our wildlife and our outdoor way of life. Protecting Idaho’s water rights from outside threats has been an article of faith — almost a religion — and any attempt by outsiders to get their hands on our water has been fighting words for all Idaho politicians regardless of political party or persuasion. Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights That’s why the Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming “supremacy” over Idaho’s water serving the Idaho National Laboratory is a gut punch to the people of Idaho. But our current political leaders, unlike those throughout history, have played a role in giving the Trump administration the notion that Idaho is a lap dog for whatever the president wants by their silence and eagerness to partner with the federal government regardless of the consequences for Idahoans, their economy and their way of life. Last summer, without informing the people of Idaho, Gov. Brad Little signed a memorandum of understanding with the Trump administration hoping that the Idaho National Laboratory could become a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and accept 33 percent of all radioactive waste generated in the country . Little has not explained how this campus and taking the waste will affect our precious water supply nor how it will impact the Snake River Aquifer, which supplies a significant amount of water to our southern Idaho farms, ranches, trout farms and cities. Other than a few comments for a story published by the Idaho Capital Sun , the governor has said little about how this major initiative will affect Idaho. Our congressional delegation has also remained silent on this issue except to say the campus will bring economic prosperity and jobs to eastern Idaho. Now, through the lawsuit the Trump administration has filed in U.S. District Court, we know that the federal government views the water it receives from Idaho as its water and that Idaho has no legal right to curtail water to INL even during one of the worse drought seasons in the state’s history. The Trump administration argues that federal installations like INL are “shielded by the supremacy clause” from state regulations unless “Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.” The Trump administration also argues, as it has while promoting the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and the radioactive waste repository, that Idaho’s decision to curtail INL’s water has “safety, economic and energy consequences.” Moreover, the Trump administration says that “curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” another way of saying it would disrupt President Trump’s quest to build nuclear reactors across the country. But the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus is but only one issue where our water could be in jeopardy and where our governor and congressional delegation have remained silent when the future of Idaho is at stake and should be debated. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) One Boise State. Five priorities. David Hahn formally began his presidency Thursday afternoon — with a call for “shared purpose” and an outline of commitments to the Boise State University community and the state. Hahn’s list of priorities includes an ambitious fundraising drive, and enhanced partnerships with Idaho employers. “One Boise State begins with our students, faculty, and staff,” Hahn said at a ceremony marking his investiture as Boise State’s eighth president. “But it extends far beyond campus.” A president’s investiture is steeped in academic tradition, and Hahn’s ceremony was steeped in Bronco culture — with performances by a Boise State choral ensemble and the Blue Thunder Marching Band, and an unannounced cameo from football coach Spencer Danielson. Thursday’s ceremony also came nearly four months into Hahn’s actual presidency; the State Board of Education hired Hahn on July 1 , bringing a turbulent 16-month job search to a conclusion. But Hahn leveraged the moment, and used a 17-minute speech, to hammer home the “one Boise State” theme. He also articulated his five goals: student success; preparing graduates for the workforce; university research; philanthropy and athletics. Hahn’s to-do list contained at least one new wrinkle. He pledged to build on Boise State’s $500 million Unbridled fundraising campaign, setting a new $700 million target with an emphasis on student opportunities, research and endowed dean’s positions. “We can do that, together,” he said. Boise State hit the $500 million target in 2025 , and Unbridled has now raised $565 million. Hahn — who came to Boise State from the University of Arizona, where he served as dean of the college of engineering — restated his commitment to research. He again pledged to pursue top-tier R1 research status through the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education, a designation that could bring more research funding to the university. He also said Boise State should put its research to work “to power and protect” Idaho. Hahn also said Boise State needs to work closely with Idaho businesses from high-tech to healthcare, with a focus on hands-on learning and internships. “Our responsibility is to prepare the next generation of talent.” Hahn doubled down on athletics. Weeks after the State Board of Education gave Boise State athletics the go-ahead to run on an $18 million deficit — and use other university funds to make up the gap — Hahn called sports an essential part of the university’s mission. Hahn said Boise State can build one of the nation’s premier athletic programs, even in a turbulent time for intercollegiate sports . “Boise State will not sit on the sidelines and wait for someone else to determine our future,” Hahn said. But Hahn said his first commitment — and his highest priority — is student success. And Hahn began his speech with a shoutout to the ceremony’s opening speaker: Ramiro Mendoza, a Boise State junior majoring in marketing.
