(Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families) It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to understand what went wrong in her pregnancy, and not until this week to realize she hadn’t fully grappled with it emotionally. Teigen, a former model and business owner, came to Idaho on Wednesday to make a final push leading up to Nov. 3 in favor of Proposition 1, the ballot measure that would restore access to abortion in Idaho. The state has a near-total ban that applies to any stage of pregnancy, with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. The initiative, if passed, would also protect access to birth control and fertility assistance treatments such as in vitro fertilization. Opponents to the measure have called the initiative too extreme because it would allow abortions up to fetal viability, which was the law in Idaho prior to the ban, with exceptions after that point when the pregnancy threatens a patient’s health or life. Prior to a rally in downtown Boise with Prop 1 volunteers and supporters, Teigen — who lived in Idaho Falls in the early 1990s — met privately at a coffee shop with 12 Idaho women who have been telling their stories for the campaign about needing abortion care in Idaho. The women sat in a circle and told brief versions of their stories: miscarriages that led to septic infections because of hesitant medical providers, travel out of state for fatal anomalies and catastrophic health complications, and memorials to the babies they lost. Nonprofit organization Idahoans United for Women and Families, which has led the campaign for the initiative, coordinated the event, and owners of Neckar Coffee donated the space and coffee. Kate Campbell spoke of her son, Remy, and the infected placenta that caused her water to break at 20 weeks and begin labor. A fetus generally can’t survive outside of the womb before 22 weeks, and every day that goes by without an abortion procedure increases the risk of a potentially life-threatening infection, which can cause organ damage and lead to fertility loss. Since Idaho’s law only allows for intervention to save a patient’s life, doctors decided not to wait until she was close to death and airlifted Campbell to Utah for care. Utah allows abortion until 18 weeks, and after that, the law includes an exception to preserve a patient’s health, not just to prevent death. “The only ‘cure,’ if you will, for an infected placenta is giving birth,” Campbell said through tears. She now has a 14-month-old daughter. A doctor at her 20-week ultrasound told her she needed to get to Utah as quickly as possible, and she and her husband, Morgan, made the five-hour drive and called multiple hospitals and clinics before they found someone who could help. “It was just horrific,” Ballis said. items.body: If you distrust government with spending and tax decisions, why would you put politicians at your state capitol in charge of more of it? That’s the question at the center of Idaho’s current debate over property taxes. There is no statewide property tax in Idaho, but local governments can collect property tax revenue. Property taxes frustrate homeowners for understandable reasons. Paying off your mortgage does not end the annual bill. A rising home value does not put cash in your checking account. For retirees and families with tight budgets, the burden can be substantial. But property taxes in Idaho are a creature of local government: schools, fire departments, cities, sewer, etc. In many cases, local voters have approved the new taxes and fees collected. If you’ve voted in favor of a bond, levy, or other local tax measure, you are partly responsible for the extra rate you might be paying. There are various ideas on how to eliminate the local property tax burden, but all of them have drawbacks. For example, we examined the concept of doing away with property taxes and, in exchange, giving local governments the option to adopt limited sales taxes. The concept is that this spreads the burden and allows visitors to cover part of the burden. It might work well in some areas but would likely be a burden too heavy to handle in others. It wasn’t a proposal; it was a thought experiment. Others have suggested you can do away with local property taxes by simply having local governments be funded by the state in Boise. In other words, they want state taxpayers to pay for local government decisions. But directing state revenue toward local property tax replacement creates two significant trade-offs: greater dependence on Boise and less room for other state tax reductions (such as the income tax). Today, local elected officials must answer to local voters for their spending and many of the taxes supporting it. The connection is imperfect, but important: Officials who approve spending should face the taxpayers expected to finance it. Under a state-funded replacement system, local officials would increasingly look to the Legislature for revenue. Instead of having to justify spending to local taxpayers, they would lobby for larger distributions from Boise. Local budgets would become more dependent on legislative formulas, negotiations, and priorities. Supporters argue that local control would survive because local officials would still decide how to spend the money. But spending authority is only part of the equation. Whoever controls the funding holds considerable power over the recipient. Future legislatures could also change it. During a downturn, lawmakers would face competing demands from state programs and local governments counting on replacement dollars. Imagine a scenario where your local government leaders are not talking to you about local spending but instead wandering the halls of the state capitol looking for revenue from legislative leaders. That’s a concentration of power that is anything but conservative. We should also carefully examine what this idea would mean for future state tax cuts. After all, the state currently collects income and sales tax revenues. If some of those revenues now have to be used for local government spending, we would likely see fewer, if any, income or sales tax cuts. The dreams some have of a grocery tax abolishment would likely go out the window. This is not to say there are not viable paths forward. Idaho can and should restrain local spending, examine overlapping taxing districts, and adopt Truth in Taxation so officials must clearly disclose and defend proposed property tax increases. Communities could also be allowed to consider voter-approved exchanges of property taxes for local sales taxes. Our study shows that approach would be more feasible in some counties than others. Any exchange should include reasonable rate limits and permanent, dollar-for-dollar reductions in property tax authority

(Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Trump administration is sending election monitors to Idaho’s largest county on Election Day next week, the state’s top election official confirmed Wednesday. The decision comes as the Justice Department plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors — who the DOJ says are meant to assess local compliance with federal voting rights laws — to all 50 states. That would make for a significantly expanded presence than under the Biden administration, which sent election monitors to 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections, States Newsroom reported. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, an elected Republican, said the U.S. Justice Department notified him and the Ada County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, that there will be two teams in Ada County on Election Day. Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple, also a Republican, said around six election monitors who are local to Idaho will be stationed near polling places — but not inside. In a statement, the Justice Department said its election monitors in Idaho and elsewhere will be “doing the routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.” “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” a spokesperson for the federal agency told the Idaho Capital Sun. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) “I’m fairly sure we’ve had it under all (presidential) administrations in some form. I can most clearly remember ADA conversations when Obama was president. But it has been routine in the past,” McGrane said in an interview. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy. At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. “If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.” In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven. The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition. Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier) “She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.” In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. Crozier’s was among them. The state of Idaho has awarded $186 million in federal rural healthcare grants — with more than $20 million going into education-related programs. On Wednesday — three days before the feds’ deadline — state officials announced that the first-year grant process was a wrap. “I’m proud of the work that brought us to this point, and I’m excited to see these investments improve care for Idaho families across our state,” said Sen. Julie VanOrden, R-Pingree, the co-chair of a legislative oversight committee that has reviewed the grant applications. Year One: Some highlights The two biggest education-related awards have been in the works for some time . About $12.5 million will go into a suite of 11 initiatives to encourage rural students to pursue healthcare careers. Most of these programs are co-ops involving multiple colleges and universities. The biggest of the group is a $4.3 million Boise State University-led mobile simulation lab project, designed to bring clinical training into rural communities. The State Board of Education will receive $8 million for graduate medical education — rural fellowships and residencies for medical school graduates. Here’s a look at some other education-related grants: The University of Idaho will receive $2 million to create a statewide chronic disease education network. Idaho State University will receive $2 million for a cognitive care pathway network. The U of I and Eat Smart Idaho will share nearly $1.6 million for chronic disease prevention and cancer screening programs. Another U of I grant, of close to $1.2 million, will go toward a pediatric psychiatric assistance line and mental and behavioral health programs. Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic, which will provide specialized hearing testing in rural Idaho. “For many Idaho families — especially in rural areas — affordable, accessible health care is a real concern,” Gov. Brad Little said in a news release touting the first-year grants. “This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they’re needed most.” Year Two funding: No news yet There was some considerable confusion Wednesday about Idaho’s second-year grant. On Wednesday, as state officials announced the wrapup of their first-year grant program, the Trump administration issued a news release that at least implied an additional $186 million was on its way. “Today, the Trump Administration announced nearly $186 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho,” the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services news release said. However, the release simply referred, again, to the first-year grant, which was awarded in December . Idaho won’t find out about its second-year grant for at least a few more weeks. The federal grants are competitive — meaning funding could increase or decrease based on a state’s first-year track record. That’s why Idaho officials and the legislative oversight committee emphasized the importance of meeting the feds’ reporting requirements and hitting the Oct. 30 grant deadline. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at. According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found. The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23. But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles. In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see. “Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway) “An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus , had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. items.body: An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season. The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say. Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness. “While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season. Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death. items.body: The College of Western Idaho says its first major fundraising campaign was a $33 million success. On Tuesday, CWI said its Powering the Treasure Valley campaign had exceeded its $30 million goal — funding capital projects and scholarships at the state’s largest community college. “This campaign has always been about our students,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in a news release Tuesday. “Every gift has helped create more opportunities for students to pursue an education, develop the skills employers need, and build a future close to home.” The campaign, launched in July 2023, will leave an imprint across CWI’s landscape. Money will go toward three capital projects on the Nampa campus: The campaign helped fund the Norco Health & Science Building and Agricultural Sciences Complex , which both opened in 2025, and the CapEd Student Success Center, a student services complex that opened earlier this year. Campaign funds will also go toward the CWI downtown Boise campus and the Micron Academic Center , which is expected to open in fall 2027. CWI says the campaign also supports student aid. Since the launch in 2023, CWI has increased its annual scholarship awards from $609,000 to more than $1 million this year. However, the completed fundraising campaign won’t support two other high-profile initiatives on CWI’s radar. This money will not go toward deferred maintenance on the recently acquired Ford Idaho Center , although college officials have said fundraising will be a component in covering the $25 million in maintenance costs. This money also will not go toward an endowment-based initiative to launch CWI’s first intercollegiate athletics programs. “When CWI launched Powering the Treasure Valley … we committed to two priorities: improving the student experience and adding capacity so we can serve more students,” college spokesman Ashley Smith said in a text Tuesday.

items.body: KUNA – The Kuna School District plans to recommend new guidance on student screen time before the end of the school year as leaders work to determine how much time students spend on computers and other devices, and what they’re doing on those devices. The effort stems from community concerns about too much student screen time, said Kuna Teaching and Learning Director Kevin Gifford. The nearby West Ada district launched a similar initiative in August. “The endgame ultimately is to have a district guidance document with clear goals for what we believe an appropriate balance of screen time would be,” Gifford said. In the meantime, the district has provided some immediate guidance for teachers. Kuna’s teacher guidance A guidance document Gifford distributed to district administrators and teachers provides three “best practices” to implement immediately: Ensure screen time is teacher-planned and directed to reduce “passive consumption.” Provide students with tech-free options during downtime. Collect data on how and when students use digital learning tools and applications. The district hasn’t collected data that clearly show how much time students spend on screens, Gifford told Idaho Education News. Still, national news coverage of instructional software i-Ready led to complaints in Kuna earlier this year, Gifford said. The new initiative to gather data and recommend new rules is, in part, to quell those concerns. Student screen time expanded during the COVID pandemic, when the district largely moved to online learning, putting students on Chromebooks at home. Six years later, district leaders wonder if they are properly balancing screen time with other activities in school. The district will begin measuring student device usage to create a live data report showing districtwide screen time averages. Gifford said the goal is to gather accurate and complete data to “tell the whole story, so that we’re not just reacting to perceptions.” Parts of the initiative start in the coming weeks. The district will guide teachers to ensure students have tech-free options during free time after completing assignments, during recess or between classes. Parents will receive a district survey asking for their opinions on device usage, but the district hasn’t determined when that will happen. Gifford feels the district is also getting ahead of the Legislature, where devices in schools have been a topic of discussion in recent years. In 2025, legislators unanimously approved a law directing school districts to limit students’ access to cellphones. In the 2026 session, lawmakers discussed artificial intelligence in schools but not screen time. Senate Bill 1227 directed the Idaho Department of Education to develop a framework for “responsible use” of AI in K-12 schools. Meanwhile, some educators are evaluating whether certain students should be on computers at all. Idaho Education Technology Association communications coordinator Will Goodman told EdNews in August that the organization plans to lobby for a ban on screens in kindergarten through third grade classrooms. “I know our Legislature is going to be looking at this very topic this year,” Gifford told Kuna trustees at the district’s October board meeting. “It’ll be good for us to be already working toward it.”

(Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center) Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rights related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. “Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” “Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.” The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. items.body: Volunteers pass boxes full of signed ballot initiative petitions through the Idaho Capitol on July 2, 2026. The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act would restore abortion access “without government interference” until fetal viability, and would protect fertility treatments and other reproductive care such as contraception. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) Chrissy Teigen will be in Boise on Wednesday to campaign in favor of Proposition 1 , which would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban laws and provide protections for the procedure. Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act , also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions. Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen) Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them. She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public. Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1. Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion. “In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.” Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death. Teigen, who lived in Idaho Falls as a teen, is married to singer and pianist John Legend. They have four children. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

She says district officials forced her to resign from her special education job at Valley View Elementary School after she reported concerns about Gavin Snow, a paraprofessional who worked for Baker at Valley
items.body: A former teacher has sued the Boise School District, saying she was made the “fall guy” over a series of sexual abuse complaints. Marianne Baker is seeking at least $10,000 from the district. She says district officials forced her to resign from her special education job at Valley View Elementary School after she reported concerns about Gavin Snow, a paraprofessional who worked for Baker at Valley View. The district has agreed to $7 million in civil settlements to Boise parents who accused Snow of sexual abuse. “(Baker) was made the ‘fall guy’ for the district’s shortcomings and negligent hiring of Gavin Snow,” according to the Oct. 1 lawsuit. “Marianne was stripped of her professional passion and has suffered immense reputational damage that will follow her for the rest of her life.” District spokesman Dan Hollar declined to comment on the lawsuit Monday, because the case is “the subject of ongoing litigation.” The lawsuit presents a timeline of Baker’s final months with the Boise district: December 2024: On three occasions, Baker observes Snow had his phone in the bathroom while helping special education students — in violation of Baker’s policy for paraprofessionals. “Marianne assumed Gavin was being insubordinate by texting during working hours,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 6-7, 2025: Noting a change in Snow’s demeanor, Baker seeks to file a report with then-Valley View Principal Rick Jordan and other officials. Jan. 7, 2025: School counselor Paula Perry announces a new no-phones-in-bathrooms policy. After the meeting, Snow follows Baker into an empty staff room. Fearing for her safety, Baker leaves the room. “It was at that point that Marianne knew Gavin had done something nefarious and/or illegal with the children of her class,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 10, 2025: Jordan and a top district official tell Baker she had done the right thing by reporting Snow, the lawsuit says, “because the detectives had found child pornography on Gavin’s phone and computer at home.” About an hour after this conversation, Baker learns that Snow had taken his own life as Boise police tried to arrest him on child sexual abuse charges. Feb. 21, 2025: The district tells Baker that she is being placed on administrative leave for failing to report child abuse, abandonment or neglect. May 8, 2025: Boise Education Association leaders Lara Luthy and Stephanie Myers tell Baker that the district would be terminating her, giving her the option to resign and receive pay and benefits through September. “Lara and Stephanie informed Marianne that if she resigned, her employment file would be ‘cleaner’ and she would be able to seek employment in a school district elsewhere,” the lawsuit says. May 13, 2025: Baker “reluctantly” signs a letter of resignation. May 20, 2025: Boise district attorney Dan Skinner files a complaint against Baker with the Professional Standards Commission, a volunteer board that can revoke or suspend teaching certificates. June 16, 2025: Baker receives a criminal summons. She is charged with two misdemeanor counts of failing to report suspected abuse. Jan. 5: Magistrate Judge David Manweiler dismisses the misdemeanor counts . That same day, district officials uploaded the PSC complaint to her employment file. In her lawsuit, Baker says she has suffered high blood pressure and anxiety and “significant depression” due to the administrative leave and resignation. She says she now works as a flight attendant and a bartender on weekends, making “significantly less” than what she earned as a teacher. Baker filed a $1 million tort claim in November , as a precursor to the lawsuit.

items.body: An Ada County judge will privately review data spreadsheets compiled by Boise State University researchers before ruling on whether the university must hand them over to an anti-abortion lobbying group. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC) — a Christian lobbying group that helped write Idaho’s restrictive abortion laws — sued Boise State , alleging that it withheld public records related to a widely cited article co-authored by two researchers affiliated with the university. The article said that obstetrician-gynecologists fled Idaho after the state’s abortion ban took effect in 2022. Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-127657" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" alt="" width="150" height="200" /> Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin In December, IFPC filed a records request seeking “all documents” and “all data” related to the article, but Boise State only provided a single, two-page spreadsheet. In a July petition to Ada County’s district court, IFPC argued that the research “must have produced a paper trail longer than two pages.” IFPC’s petition asked the court to compel the university to hand over additional records, including emails along with documents from Boise State’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), which approved the researchers’ process for collecting data on human subjects. District Judge Nancy Baskin heard arguments in the case Friday. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, represented Boise State. While Peterson acknowledged that additional records related to the article exist, including various other data sets, he argued that the university reviewed IFPC’s request “in good faith” and provided the only record that matched its request. After asking the attorneys questions for more than an hour, Baskin ordered Boise State to show her any data files that the university deemed outside the scope of IFPC’s request. Baskin will review the spreadsheets “in-camera,” meaning behind closed doors, before she issues a written ruling on IFPC’s petition. Boise State has 10 days to deliver the spreadsheets to Baskin. Article heavily cited in debate over abortion laws The article, published last year by the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), reported that 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024 — after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, triggering Idaho’s abortion ban. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, a private law firm representing Boise State. (Photo credit: Hawley Troxell) Two researchers affiliated with Boise State — J. Edward McEachern, an adjunct faculty member and doctor at St. Luke’s, and Allen Traylor, a graduate student — co-authored the article with a doctor unaffiliated with the university. They conducted three “ cross-sectional censuses” of OB-GYN physicians practicing obstetrics in Idaho to determine how many left the state after the U.S. Supreme Court decision. The article has been frequently cited in coverage detailing the effects of Idaho’s abortion ban, including by the New York Times last week, and by supporters of Proposition 1.

(Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. Recovery centers provide support to adults, but many of those adults are parents, Smith Hansen said, and better outcomes for those adults can lead to better outcomes for their children. The money would be used to work with recovery centers statewide to develop standards, a process for accreditation and standardized metrics to evaluate outcomes. Foundation for the Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency seeks $28K to help train workforce The Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency has held a yearly conference for more than 40 years for behavioral healthcare workers, but participation is lagging and workers statewide aren’t always able to travel to the Treasure Valley for the conference, according to Leah Kalk, a board member of the foundation. Rep. Marco Erickson, R-Idaho Falls, makes a phone call from the House floor on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The foundation is seeking $28,000 for scholarships for healthcare workers statewide to travel to the conference and earn required continuing education credits. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” “This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. “I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” “The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. We will continue to focus on the work and provide quality, efficient, and effective services for the people of Idaho.” Before joining Idaho’s health agency, Charron held leadership positions in the Texas Medicaid program and with the Texas Office of Inspector General. She also worked in government programs and “compliance roles” for a community-based health plan in Arizona, according to her biography . Charron leaves Idaho’s largest agency with the biggest budget The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare runs public assistance programs like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Women and Infant Children program. The health department also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, provides child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. As head of the agency, Charron oversaw some of the beginning stages of the state’s shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies , as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345 . The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. Charron has also overseen the influx of federal funds from the Rural Health Transformation Grant. items.body: From left to right: Coeur d'Alene attorney Arthur "Art" Macomber, former Idaho Congressman Raúl Labrador and incumbent Idaho Attorney General Lawrence Wasden debate on Idaho Public Television on April 19, 2022. (Photo by Aaron Kunz/Idaho Public Television) During the 2026 election cycle, Idaho voters have had very few opportunities to see Republican incumbents answer questions at live, public events. For years it was the norm for major candidates in statewide and federal races to appear live and debate each other. Journalist Betsy Z. Russell asks a candidate question during an Idaho Public Television debate on May 6, 2016. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger) “It was a tradition in Idaho,” said Betsy Russell, former longtime president of the Idaho Press Club and current president for Idahoans for Openness in Government. “That was how candidates, including incumbents seeking reelection, got out there and put their views and how they contrasted with those of their opponents, in front of all voters all across the state of Idaho.” Idaho Public Television, which for years has broadcast its Idaho Debates series statewide, did not have the staffing to put on the events this year, according to Melissa Davlin, IPTV producer and Idaho Press Club president. “I do think there are some incumbents who would have said yes to debates had that been a possibility,” Davlin said. Davlin also noted that there’s a national trend of candidates from both major parties declining debates. Of the 35 U.S. Senate seats up for election this year, 21 of them had no debate between the major candidates, ABC News reported. items.body: Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios, but high costs to build such projects can create barriers. (Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA) High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate. “When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.” Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power) “On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit. The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor. None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. “The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said.
